title: Direct inguinal operative anatomy

cues.phrase: The cord enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; the femoral vessels pass below the ligament.
cues.why: The accessibility description teaches where both distractor targets lie. Together with X being medial and above, a reader can eliminate the named deep-ring and femoral choices spatially without knowing the deficient layer. The visible drawing also labels these two alternative locations.

cues.phrase: No defect classification is labelled.
cues.why: Editorial commentary advertises the intended classification exercise; it supplies no patient information.

fairness: The transversalis-fascia target is defensible for the depicted direct defect, but identifying a familiar location and naming its wall layer is essentially one anatomy association, not two consequential decisions. Too easy for PGY-2/3 residents.

Importance: high-yield groin anatomy. Realism: the schematic exists and is legible; retrospective clinic review is plausible, although the choices describe simplified targets rather than complete repairs. No definite key error identified.
suggestions: Retain the necessary orientation landmarks, but remove the explanatory distractor-location sentence and editorial assurance from the description. Keep equivalent accessible spatial observations.

Test a consequential intraoperative decision with credible neighboring repair choices and findings that change that decision, or request explicit acceptance as a foundational anatomy item. Do not merely relabel location recognition as two-step reasoning.

title: Postoperative distension cross-sectional assessment

cues.phrase: the pancreatic bed and intervening bowel are obscured by gas
cues.why: Paired with a repeat-ultrasound alternative, this explicitly names the inadequacy of that modality; CT becomes the familiar broad survey choice.

fairness: Contrast CT is a defensible next hospital study for the worsening postoperative course. The actual key does not require interpreting why output fell: postoperative pain/distension with incompletely visualized operative anatomy already selects it.

Importance: high-yield postoperative complication assessment. Realism: an urgent hospital assessment is sensible, but the presentation never explicitly locates the return visit; an unwell postoperative patient should not appear to undergo a leisurely clinic workup. Too easy for the intended resident level; MRCP and venous Doppler are weak competitors without ductal or vascular findings.
suggestions: Make a specific unresolved leak, drain-position, collection or vascular question drive the next protocol after an initial study, and compare clinically plausible protocols at that same stage.
Keep the ultrasound limitation if it is decision-critical; replace the weak alternatives rather than hide why ultrasound is inadequate. Specify the hospital escalation context.

title: Postoperative fluid composition

cues.phrase: Fluid became opaque after feeding
cues.why: Repeats the feeding-linked cloudiness already in the presentation, reinforcing the classic chyle association instead of adding a new discriminator.

cues.phrase: no gas within the collection
cues.why: An option-directed negative reduces the apparent infection alternative, although absence of gas does not exclude infection.

cues.phrase: no organisms seen on the initial stain
cues.why: A second infection-directed negative further steers the interpretation; culture is appropriately retained in every option, so this negative does little to distinguish the offered panels.

fairness: Triglyceride testing is plausible, but amylase plus culture is also clinically indicated after dissection beside the pancreatic tail. Chylous and pancreatic leakage or infection need not be mutually exclusive. 'Best addresses ... findings' does not establish why only one of these incomplete panels is the right next workup.

Importance: useful postoperative fluid assessment, although the current item is classic syndrome-to-test recall. Realism: existing aliquots and retrospective review are plausible; bilirubin testing is a weak rival in this operative location. Too easy as recognition, yet insufficiently bounded as a complete diagnostic plan.
suggestions: Ask a narrowly defined specimen-composition question, or show already-obtained clinically indicated analyses and require an integrated action that differs for mixed versus isolated leakage.

Do not imply that triglycerides substitute for pancreatic-leak assessment. Remove duplicated feeding chronology and redundant infection negatives; keep culture indications and any needed safety findings.

title: Nutrition for postoperative chylous leakage

cues.phrase: assessed energy requirement
cues.why: The task and table make 100% delivery an explicit selection criterion, eliminating plans C and D without medical knowledge.

cues.phrase: Formula after change
cues.why: That row reports rising output on exactly the 100%/30-g-long-chain/5-g-MCT composition repeated by plan B. A nonmedical reader can reject the unchanged unsuccessful plan, leaving A.

fairness: The intended adequate-energy, lower-long-chain-fat plan is plausible. However, calories and fat composition changed together, so this record alone cannot establish which change caused the output rise; avoid presenting the sequence as proof of mechanism.

Importance: practical chyle-leak nutrition, but the four-row puzzle adds little resident discrimination. Realism: dietitian comparison is plausible; exact hypothetical gram amounts must not be treated as universal prescriptions. Two independent-looking columns collapse to simple elimination. Too easy.
suggestions: Compare nutritionally adequate plans with credible differences in route or composition, and make a documented response or complication alter the next action.
Keep energy adequacy clinically relevant without making half the answers explicit underfeeding. Avoid a distractor that simply reproduces the just-failed formula. Retain the constructed-data label.

title: Nutrition during prolonged postoperative ileus

cues.phrase: Recurrent distension and vomiting; feeds returned to the previous rate
cues.why: Directly supplies why the increase-feeds option has already failed.

cues.phrase: anticipated several more days of restricted delivery
cues.why: Preinterprets persistence and rehearses why waiting at the current rate is inadequate.

cues.phrase: Add parenteral nutrition to the prescribed tube regimen
cues.why: Only the key remedies the conspicuous large deficit while preserving the only tolerated route; alternatives repeat the failed escalation or leave the deficit unchanged.

fairness: Supplemental PN is defensible in this malnourished patient with persistent inadequate delivery. The current rate, target and trajectory are useful clinical facts, but they eliminate both distractors almost verbatim; there is little remaining judgment.

Importance: very high-yield perioperative nutrition. Realism: inpatient decision reviewed later in clinic is coherent. The task should distinguish historical care from a present clinic order. Too easy for PGY-2/3 residents; no definite key error identified.
suggestions: Retain actual intake and intolerance, but compare credible supplemental-PN/enteral strategies rather than a known failed rate increase and prolonged severe underfeeding.
If timing is the objective, supply the verified time-course and nutritional-risk criteria and test a genuine near-boundary decision without inventing thresholds.

title: Mesh after a controlled enterotomy
fairness: One defensible best implant among these options: the learner must interpret the controlled contamination, viable repair and separable retromuscular plane, then apply material selection rather than reflexively choose biologic mesh. The observations are necessary eligibility information, not an answer-label match.

Importance: high-yield abdominal-wall practice and examination content. Realism: a single-stage intraoperative implant decision reviewed in clinic is credible; options name parallel, specific implants. The record does not imply that every enterotomy mandates immediate synthetic mesh.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. This is an offline editorial judgment, not verification of current comparative evidence or clinical approval.
suggestions: Retain the controlled contamination and tissue-plane details and have Melissa confirm the exact mesh-material ranking for the stated operative circumstances. No wording repair is required for editorial acceptance.

title: Meckel resection extent

cues.phrase: The pale disrupted areas extended around the base onto both sides of the ileal tube.
cues.why: The presentation supplies the full extent before the schematic is interpreted. With both opposing walls involved, the only whole-segment resection is the obvious coverage answer.

cues.phrase: Disrupted wall is marked around the diverticular base and on both the antimesenteric and opposite mesenteric sides of an adjacent ileal segment.
cues.why: The necessary accessible description reinforces the same coverage puzzle; wedge and base-only excision cannot encompass the explicitly bilateral extent. This is not a reason to remove accessible findings.

fairness: Segmental resection is defensible for this distribution, but the key also commits to primary anastomosis without circulation, contamination or remaining bowel-perfusion context. 'Healthy' ends in the drawing do not establish all reconstruction conditions.

Importance: useful general-surgery resection judgment. Realism: the image exists and is readable, but 'pale/disrupted' conflates observations with different implications; specify the actual operative wall injury or viability finding. Too easy as a lesion-coverage exercise.
suggestions: Ask resection extent without adding an unsupported reconstruction commitment, or supply the observations required to choose anastomosis.

Use a plausible wedge-versus-segmental near-miss requiring interpretation of base involvement and resulting lumen/viability. Remove redundant prose that answers the image task, while retaining accessible observations.

title: Celiac serology when IgA is deficient
fairness: The balanced two-by-two choices avoid convergence. IgA deficiency invalidates the reassuring IgA result, while gluten withdrawal separately limits a repeat antibody evaluation. The learner must address both assay selection and testing conditions; neither answer component is uniquely repeated or explained in the stem.
Importance: useful diagnostic-validity and nutrition content, though less central to operative general surgery than the perioperative items. Realism: plausible in a surgical nutrition clinic.

The key is defensible among the offered blood-testing plans. It does not establish a complete celiac diagnostic pathway or a universal gluten-challenge regimen; suitability and supervision require clinical review. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline.
suggestions: Keep both competing validity problems and the balanced options. At clinical sign-off, confirm how supervised gluten reintroduction is represented; do not add an unsupported dose or duration.

title: Celiac testing after gluten withdrawal

cues.phrase: Continue gluten avoidance, then repeat serology and biopsies
cues.why: Repeats the same testing conditions already associated with negative studies, making this an obvious stale-workup foil.

cues.phrase: then diagnose disease if HLA-DQ2 is found
cues.why: The categorical diagnosis promise makes the HLA option an overclaim rather than a credible use of susceptibility testing.

fairness: The keyed sequence is reasonable, but HLA testing can be a useful preliminary strategy in someone already avoiding gluten; the offered version is made wrong by its appended diagnostic claim. Thus the item evades the real sequencing competition.

Importance: useful testing-validity principle, but overlaps substantially with the IgA-deficiency item. Realism: clinic reassessment is credible. This is essentially one rule about testing during gluten exposure; the negative biopsy adds repetition, not a second consequential inference. Too easy.
suggestions: Offer a clinically legitimate HLA-first strategy rather than 'positive equals diagnosis', and provide the patient-specific context or existing typing result needed to rank it against a supervised challenge.
Merge overlapping celiac testing objectives if a distinct practical decision cannot be established; do not withhold relevant testing conditions to simulate difficulty.

title: Positive celiac susceptibility typing

cues.phrase: The complete specimen list from an outside mucosal-biopsy procedure identifies antral mucosa and esophageal squamous tissue.
cues.why: The conspicuous wrong-site specimen list points to the only option that obtains tissue at a new intestinal site.

cues.phrase: Assay panel for repeat tTG-IgA and endomysial IgA
cues.why: The word 'repeat' and already-positive tTG make this look like redundant work, while the key is the only tissue acquisition.

fairness: Duodenal biopsy is a defensible next step, but the HLA result is largely decorative: the same answer follows from symptoms, positive tTG with normal IgA, and lack of duodenal sampling. The title's susceptibility-typing construct is not meaningfully assessed.

Importance: moderately useful diagnostic-workup content; weaker general-surgery yield than the other nutrition questions. Realism: an outside endoscopy can miss the relevant target, but the record should make clear why that endoscopy was performed. Too easy; the tissue versus assay category split assists selection.
suggestions: Choose whether the objective is interpreting HLA or obtaining adequate duodenal tissue. For the latter, compare credible specimen/acquisition strategies with an actual adequacy discrepancy; for the former, make HLA change the next decision.
Avoid using two blood panels as disposable foils for the sole biopsy choice. Consider merging with the other celiac diagnostic-validity items.

title: HCC tumor burden versus liver resection suitability
fairness: The learner must distinguish limited tumor burden from liver functional reserve and clinically important portal hypertension, then prioritize a pathway addressing both. A small solitary tumor makes resection or ablation initially credible; repeated ascites drainage and varices change the ranking.

Importance: high-yield HPB decision-making. Realism: an outpatient transplant referral discussion is appropriate. 'Assessment' rather than guaranteed transplantation properly leaves candidacy evaluation open.

Transplant-center assessment is the best priority among the options. Ablation could still have a bridging or alternative role; the question should not imply that choosing assessment prohibits it. No definite key error identified offline.
suggestions: Preserve the tumor-versus-liver-function tension and the word 'prioritized'. Have clinical sign-off retain the distinction between referral priority, final candidacy and possible bridging treatment.

title: Structural assessment before gastric emptying

cues.phrase: The scope stopped proximal to the narrowing.
cues.why: Names the incomplete inspection that the key proposes to finish.

cues.phrase: The specimen log identifies tissue from a prepyloric erosion, while CT describes focal thickening at the narrowing.
cues.why: The overt sample/lesion mismatch steers to the only option that includes lesion biopsy. It is clinically relevant, but combined with nonbiopsy competitors largely announces the missing action.

fairness: Importance: high-yield distinction between mechanical outlet obstruction and a motility diagnosis. The intended two steps are recognizing that diabetes does not establish gastroparesis and resolving an inadequately sampled structural lesion.

Fairness concern: the record does not explain why the first scope stopped or what makes a second endoscopy feasible and diagnostically superior now. Contrast fluoroscopy can be a defensible next anatomical study after an incompletely traversed outlet. I cannot confidently rank that sequence without more acquisition/obstruction context.

Realism: retained food, narrowing and focal thickening are credible. Repeat inspection and tissue sampling may be appropriate, but the needed preparation or altered technique is not specified; do not infer it from the key.
suggestions: Give the actual reason the first examination was limited and the observations establishing safe, useful repeat access. Specify the repeat diagnostic protocol if it differs materially.
Compare credible approaches to the unresolved lesion at the same stage, and retain the distinction between prepyloric tissue and the actual target without turning it into a missing-biopsy slogan.

title: Reassessing nutrition after ileus resolves

cues.phrase: the supplements she actually consumed
cues.why: Emphasizes exactly which numbers the reader should add, preempting the proposed counting error.

cues.phrase: Retain PN as the primary route; reduce meals and supplements
cues.why: Makes the competing plan reduce a tolerated route that already supplies the target, so it is weak even without detailed nutrition knowledge.

cues.phrase: Replace the drinks with postpyloric tube feeding
cues.why: Adds an invasive route despite explicitly tolerated meals and consumed drinks. This is a category/invasiveness cue rather than a close clinical alternative.

fairness: The oral totals exceed the stated energy and protein targets, and PN withdrawal is defensible. The table is basic addition, followed by an obvious route choice; it does not meet the intended resident difficulty.

Importance: high-yield transition off PN. Realism: a dietitian intake audit is appropriate in recovery clinic. No definite clinical error identified, but the task should distinguish withdrawing the prescription from any particular tapering or glucose-monitoring protocol. Too easy.
suggestions: Compare plausible PN reduction or withdrawal plans with the same oral regimen, using an intake trajectory or clinically relevant limitation that changes the decision.
Remove the didactic emphasis on 'actually consumed'; keep recorded delivered intake as neutral data. Avoid making tube feeding a foil when oral tolerance is unambiguously established.

title: Incidental gallbladder muscle invasion

cues.phrase: the cystic-duct margin is free of tumor
cues.why: This directly weakens the duct-stump re-excision distractor. It is necessary operative-planning information, however, and does not select completion resection over surveillance without interpreting invasion depth.

fairness: The learner must reinterpret the histological layer despite the original 'superficial' label, then distinguish completion oncologic assessment from surveillance. The key requests specialist assessment rather than declaring an operation inevitable.
Importance: high-yield incidental gallbladder-cancer management. Realism: specialist slide review, staging and functional assessment fit a postoperative clinic visit.

The key is defensible among these choices. T1b completion-resection recommendations and patient-specific tradeoffs require clinician confirmation; offline editorial PASS is not a claim that all evidence is uniform. The negative duct margin is a justified cue, not a reason to omit a necessary finding.
suggestions: Retain the raw muscle-invasion finding and specialist-assessment framing. Preserve margin and staging information. Confirm the exact completion-resection recommendation at clinical sign-off.

title: Gastric cancer with adjacent-organ invasion

cues.phrase: tumor entering the splenic hilum
cues.why: Nearly names the organ to remove.

cues.phrase: The pancreatic tail separated along a soft tissue plane with an intact surface.
cues.why: Nearly names the organ to preserve. With the four binary combinations, the two sentences directly assemble the key.

fairness: The intended splenectomy with pancreatic preservation is defensible if the operative observations establish splenic-hilar involvement and no pancreatic invasion. The balanced matrix avoids convergence, but the case gives both component conclusions almost explicitly.

Importance: useful gastric-cancer principle against unnecessary adjacent-organ resection. Realism: discussing an intraoperative assessment as the 'operative plan' in clinic is temporally awkward; frame it clearly as retrospective review. Too easy for residents; no independent second decision is required.
suggestions: Use an actual uncertainty in adjacent-organ adherence or invasion and compare concrete oncologic plans that require interpreting that finding. Do not invent a reason to sacrifice an uninvolved organ.
Alternatively retain as an explicitly accepted foundational organ-preservation item. Clarify that the operative findings are being reviewed after surgery.

title: Mammographic mass morphology
fairness: Mass B is the best priority: the learner must interpret suspicious morphology in light of interval change and surgical-bed stability rather than choose high density or palpability alone. Each competing target has a plausible concerning feature, and the same action is offered at each site.

Importance: high-yield breast-workup reasoning. Realism: radiologist correlation and interval comparison are credible in surgical clinic. A table is appropriate for the longitudinal comparison, though it is not a substitute for a validated visual-morphology exercise.

Priority is defensible, but it does not establish that the enlarging palpable mass C needs no sampling. The unspecified magnitude and interval of growth limit any stronger claim about C; no confident key error identified for the narrowly prioritized task.
suggestions: Keep the task limited to priority and have clinical sign-off explicitly retain any separate workup needed for C. Do not convert this into a single-biopsy-only policy.

title: Calcification morphology and distribution

cues.phrase: No target calcifications in specimen; clip anterior to the mapped group
cues.why: Only group A is explicitly unsampled; the task asks which group needs renewed targeting. A reader can match missing target to repeat sampling without interpreting calcification morphology.

cues.phrase: Target calcifications present; clip centered on the sampled group
cues.why: Both competing groups are explicitly described as successfully targeted; their pathology also explains the calcifications. This completes option-by-option elimination.

fairness: Repeat targeting of A is appropriate, but morphology and the DCIS diagnosis are largely unnecessary to identify the stated technical miss. The answer follows from specimen coverage alone.

Importance: high-yield radiology-pathology concordance. Realism: specimen radiographs and clip maps are appropriate; clip location by itself can be misleading, but absent target calcifications independently supports inadequacy here. Too easy for PGY-2/3 residents.
suggestions: Test a genuine concordance decision after apparently successful sampling, with plausible competing interpretations of what was represented, rather than making only one row explicitly miss its target.
Keep specimen calcification data and avoid treating clip displacement alone as proof of failed acquisition. Remove redundant reassurance for the other rows unless it changes the decision.

title: Palpable breast mass in the thirties

cues.phrase: the 3-o'clock palpable site is not shown
cues.why: Explicitly identifies the missing site. Two options repeat that site and two repeat the known wrong site, so half the choices are eliminated without medical knowledge.

cues.phrase: Diagnostic mammography and ultrasound at 12 o'clock
cues.why: Repeats the prior wrong target as a complete alternative even though the task explicitly asks about the current palpable finding.

cues.phrase: Contrast breast MRI and ultrasound at 12 o'clock
cues.why: A second deliberately wrong-site choice pads the matrix. The remaining decision is a straightforward first-line modality rule.

fairness: Diagnostic mammography with targeted ultrasound is defensible in this nonpregnant 36-year-old. The study/site discrepancy is important but not difficult when the mismatch is fully announced.

Importance: high-yield breast evaluation. Realism: referral-site errors are possible, but two obvious wrong-site plans are not credible resident decisions. Too easy; no definite clinical error identified.
suggestions: Put the correct current site in every option and compare credible next diagnostic plans based on actual mammographic/sonographic findings or discordance.
If wrong-site recognition is deliberately tested as a safety item, seek explicit acceptance of that easy role instead of presenting a four-choice matrix as resident-level two-step reasoning.

title: Benign phyllodes excision planning

cues.phrase: Benign: complete excision without a prescribed fixed-width rim.
cues.why: The stem states the rule needed to answer; no phyllodes knowledge is required.

cues.phrase: cut crosses the capsule where the narrow extension begins
cues.why: Directly declares plan A incomplete under the supplied rule.

cues.phrase: removes the least tissue while meeting the stated policy
cues.why: The task selects the smaller of the two complete maps. Plan C additionally sacrifices the nipple-areolar complex, making B the obvious least-harm option.

fairness: B is uniquely correct under the provided policy and constructed maps. Fairness is achieved by turning the exercise into reading comprehension rather than resident-level clinical reasoning.

Importance: complete benign-phyllodes excision is useful, but this policy/map exercise has lower incremental yield within a batch containing numerous phyllodes margin items. Realism: surgical contour planning is plausible; exact millimeter cut maps imply more certainty than an actual preoperative plan. The task introduces 'left-breast' without earlier laterality, a minor continuity gap.
suggestions: Merge with a postoperative specimen-completeness decision or test a clinically meaningful capsular/extent uncertainty using comparable specific surgical plans.

If a policy excerpt is necessary because recommendations differ, retain it but require interpretation beyond selecting the smallest qualifying number. Remove irrelevant borderline/malignant policy clauses from a purely benign task.

title: Benign phyllodes margin after excision
fairness: The learner must distinguish tumor at ink from a transected or visibly residual benign lesion, then avoid automatically applying carcinoma margin or radiation rules. The benign grade and intact-excision observations are necessary, not a paraphrase of the surveillance label.
Importance: useful breast-surgery practice, although less central than common breast malignancy decisions. Realism: postoperative pathology/operative/imaging reconciliation fits the clinic setting.

Surveillance is defensible for the specified intact benign excision. Re-excision can still be discussed in individualized care; the broad wording 'should be discussed' is less exclusive than 'recommended next plan'. Exact management requires Melissa's confirmation; no certain clinical error identified. Preserve this frozen version rather than silently edit it.
suggestions: Retain the exact frozen item. Record the discussion-versus-recommendation wording limitation for manager/clinical review rather than changing the passed version in this batch.

title: Borderline phyllodes close-margin action

cues.phrase: Borderline: aim 5 mm; below 3 mm supports re-excision.
cues.why: The pre-answer policy states the exact action rule.

cues.phrase: Final reported margin
cues.why: The final column has already reconciled the main specimen and shaves. Reading its sole value below 3 mm gives the key; interpreting specimen coverage is unnecessary.

cues.phrase: No lateral shave in the specimen log
cues.why: Reinforces the only residual close-margin site and points directly to the lateral re-excision option.

fairness: Lateral re-excision follows the supplied policy and final site-specific report. The superior shave is described as covering the full face, so there is no demonstrated residual ambiguity. However, the item counts an interpretation already performed by the pathologist as learner reasoning.

Importance: useful margin reconciliation, but repetitive within this phyllodes-heavy batch. Realism: an oriented reconciliation is credible; exact combined margin reporting needs pathologist confirmation. Too easy for residents.
suggestions: Test a real specimen-orientation or coverage discrepancy that changes the remaining operation, using clinically validated reporting conventions. Do not simply delete a necessary final margin and ask the learner to invent one.
Alternatively merge the borderline target and close-margin items into one meaningful planning decision. Keep any policy needed for fairness, but avoid a task solvable by reading one final number.

title: Malignant phyllodes close-margin action

cues.phrase: Malignant: aim 10 mm; below 5 mm supports re-excision.
cues.why: The stem gives the exact rule selecting surgery for the stated 4-mm margin.

cues.phrase: changes the grade to malignant phyllodes; the measured posterior margin remains 4 mm
cues.why: The current grade and number directly plug into the supplied rule; the old grade is not needed to answer the present task.

cues.phrase: should replace
cues.why: Presupposes that the earlier surveillance plan must change, further weakening the surveillance alternative before clinical reasoning.

fairness: Under the supplied policy, posterior re-excision is the intended best recommendation. But the posterior surface is not anatomically characterized: available breast tissue, fascia or chest-wall boundary can affect the actual re-excision decision. The item should not imply a universal mandate independent of that anatomy.

Importance: clinically relevant response to upgraded pathology, but a rare-tumor rule lookup has limited incremental resident yield alongside the other phyllodes tasks. Realism: specialist grade revision is credible. Too easy despite the chronology.
suggestions: Use a neutral 'current local-control plan' task and give the actual posterior operative boundary relevant to further surgery.

Require reconciliation of a substantive grade/extent or specimen issue before applying a policy; avoid merely stating the new grade and action threshold. Compare plausible local-control plans at the same stage.

title: Axillary surgery in phyllodes

cues.phrase: without a separate epithelial carcinoma
cues.why: Explicitly excludes the common competing reason for axillary staging.

cues.phrase: no additional axillary target is described
cues.why: An author-level assurance discourages any further axillary procedure.

cues.phrase: Nodal tissue with preserved architecture and reactive follicles; no malignant cells
cues.why: The already-benign interpretation, combined with repeated matching-target and stability assurances, makes no axillary intervention the conspicuously conservative choice.

cues.phrase: radiology and pathology identify the same target
cues.why: States the concordance conclusion the proposed interpretation task would otherwise require.

fairness: No routine axillary staging is defensible in malignant phyllodes with a satisfactorily evaluated reactive node. Necessary benign sampling findings should not be withheld. The problem is that the item supplies the adequacy/concordance conclusions and then tests a familiar single rule.

Importance: useful distinction from epithelial breast carcinoma; eight related phyllodes items have diminishing practical yield. Realism: the target log is plausible, but repeated exclusions are editorial over-scaffolding. Too easy.
suggestions: Retain enough target and tissue observations to establish adequacy, but remove repeated author assurances and require the learner to resolve a meaningful discordance.
Compare clinically credible axillary next steps rather than using full dissection as an unsupported foil. Consider merging with the suspicious-node item.

title: A suspicious node in phyllodes

cues.phrase: the post-biopsy clip lies in fat next to the node; no nodal tissue is reported
cues.why: Directly announces the miss. The key is the only choice that samples the actual node now.

cues.phrase: Excision biopsy centered on the existing axillary clip
cues.why: Deliberately targets the object the stem just placed outside the node; this is an obvious wrong-target choice without needing medical knowledge.

fairness: A properly targeted needle biopsy is defensible. The combination of clip location and no nodal tissue supports a failed sample; the problem is not missing data but a caricatured surgical alternative. True excision of the enlarging node could be a reasonable competing approach, depending on accessibility and diagnostic needs.
Importance: high-value general specimen-target concordance principle, more useful than phyllodes-specific recall. Realism: an off-target needle sample is plausible. Too easy as currently phrased.
suggestions: Offer actual node excision rather than excision of a known misplaced clip, and supply accessibility/architecture needs that allow a defensible comparison with repeat image-guided biopsy.
Keep the inadequate-sample evidence; make the next action a real choice instead of restating the missed target.

title: Borderline phyllodes operative margin target

cues.phrase: Borderline: aim 5 mm; below 3 mm supports re-excision.
cues.why: Provides the numerical selection rule before the answer.

cues.phrase: with the least additional breast-tissue sacrifice
cues.why: Once map A's 2-mm surface is rejected, the task tells the reader to choose B over the uniformly wider C without clinical knowledge.

cues.phrase: Removes the lateral extension; retains nipple base
cues.why: Only the key's consequence is framed as resolving the extension while preserving a desirable structure; C is framed as extra central-tissue removal.

fairness: B satisfies the constructed policy/map comparison. There is a continuity issue: the presentation says each map removes the lesion, but only B's consequence says it removes 'the lateral extension', which can imply A leaves tumor. Clarify whether that extension is tumor or a planned margin extension.

Importance: initial phyllodes margin planning is useful but this duplicates other supplied-policy tasks and has low incremental yield. Realism: prescribed surgical aims are not guaranteed final histological margins. Too easy.
suggestions: Clarify what each map actually contains and distinguish planned rim from final pathological clearance.

Merge with a margin-management item unless a different consequential decision can be shown. Retain policy access when needed, but remove the smallest-qualifying-number puzzle and compare realistic operations with supported tradeoffs.

title: Malignant phyllodes operative margin target

cues.phrase: Malignant: aim 10 mm; below 5 mm supports re-excision.
cues.why: Gives the initial target directly; reading the minimum rim in each row is sufficient.

cues.phrase: while avoiding the additional chest-wall resection shown
cues.why: The task explicitly rules out map C, the only row naming an additional pectoral-muscle segment.

cues.phrase: Breast tissue plus the planned posterior extension
cues.why: The key is presented as the middle amount of tissue removal, exactly matching the instructed target-without-extra-sacrifice rule.

fairness: B is uniquely selected by the stipulated map and policy, but no medical reasoning is required. The difference between initial counseling aim and postoperative re-excision threshold is useful; here the stem and task do all of that interpretation.

Importance: limited incremental value beside the borderline-target and malignant-close-margin items. Realism: posterior tissue planes are insufficiently defined to generalize whether a specified extra rim is achievable without chest-wall resection. Too easy.
suggestions: Replace the explicit avoidance instruction with a neutral operative-planning task and a clinically grounded posterior-plane problem.

Consider merging the initial-target and postoperative-margin distinction into one clinically realistic case. Do not create difficulty by hiding the applicable policy or pretending an exact planned rim guarantees final clearance.

title: Phyllodes dissemination pattern
fairness: The learner must recognize that a distant lesion can change curative-intent breast planning, then prioritize tissue that distinguishes metastasis from a separate lung primary. Prior lung adenocarcinoma makes histology genuinely consequential; the three choices are parallel tissue acquisitions.

Importance: high-yield oncologic staging principle, though the phyllodes-specific setting is uncommon. Realism: clinic staging before proposed local treatment is credible. A peripheral pulmonary target makes image-guided acquisition plausible without an artificial availability assurance.

Pulmonary sampling is the best priority among these options if technically feasible. Actual lesion size, accessibility and biopsy risk would matter in practice, and staging other suspicious sites is not excluded. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline.
suggestions: Retain the competing prior malignancy and curative-intent consequence. At clinical sign-off, confirm that the proposed lung target is safely accessible and that priority does not imply abandoning the node or breast-bed workup.

title: Overt renin-independent aldosterone production

cues.phrase: CT-directed unilateral adrenalectomy planning
cues.why: This option extends beyond the task's 'endocrine testing pathway' into an operation and can be partly rejected by category. It does not distinguish the key from the credible suppression-testing alternative.

cues.phrase: Potassium was corrected and interfering medicines were managed for his endocrine testing.
cues.why: An interpreted preparation assurance removes potential assay confounders. It is a fair boundary for this downstream objective, but it means the learner is not being tested on preparation adequacy.

fairness: The consequential distinctions are whether this overt biochemical phenotype warrants bypassing suppression testing and whether imaging can replace functional lateralization before surgery. Exact assay-dependent criteria make this a challenging PGY-2/3 item, not merely a diagnosis-label match.

Importance: high-yield endocrine-surgery pathway selection. Realism: explicit surgical preference is relevant because it changes the value of lateralization testing; it is not gratuitous preference cueing.

The key is defensible under the intended overt-phenotype pathway. Current assay-specific thresholds and exceptions were not independently verified because network use is prohibited; Melissa must confirm them. The category cue above does not determine the answer between the two actual testing sequences. Preserve the frozen version.
suggestions: Retain the exact frozen item and flag the testing-versus-operative-planning category limitation for future manager review. Do not imply that CT alone establishes unilateral functional disease or that this editorial PASS clinically approves the numerical criteria.

title: Factor assessment after an inhibitory mixing pattern
fairness: Immediate correction followed by loss of correction after incubation, with a normal incubated control, requires interpretation of a time-dependent inhibitory pattern. The next panel then tests the specific clinically plausible inhibitor rather than assuming a simple factor deficiency or choosing lupus-anticoagulant testing reflexively.

Importance: high-yield perioperative coagulation and acquired bleeding-disorder assessment. Realism: bruising, a peripheral redraw and laboratory interference checks fit preoperative evaluation; hematology involvement is appropriate.

Factor VIII activity plus inhibitor testing is the defensible priority. The mixing result is not itself definitive diagnosis, and lupus-anticoagulant testing can still be useful in a broader workup. Parallel panels and shared factor VIII testing avoid length/category/convergence cues. No definite clinical error identified offline.
suggestions: Retain the immediate/incubated/control pattern and frame the selected panel as the next priority with hematology, not the only testing ever needed.

title: New swelling despite established lymphedema

cues.phrase: the femoral and popliteal segments were not examined because the requested study was a limited calf protocol
cues.why: Explicitly names the missing proximal coverage, while the key is 'Complete proximal-leg venous duplex ultrasound'. The absent-coverage-to-complete-test match solves the item.

cues.phrase: New thigh tenderness and increased whole-leg circumference
cues.why: Repeats the proximal distribution already described in the presentation, reinforcing the only proximal-leg test over two pelvic studies.

fairness: Prompt proximal venous assessment is defensible despite chronic lymphedema. The calf-only protocol is an unusual way to describe a DVT exclusion study and needs realism review; an actual acquisition record should justify it rather than invent a conspicuous omission for the question.

Importance: very high-yield avoidance of diagnostic anchoring after surgery. Realism: clinic escalation can be appropriate, but a symptomatic postoperative patient needs a prompt pathway. No definite key error; difficulty is too low because both distractors bypass the directly identified missing examination.
suggestions: Use a realistic ultrasound acquisition/quality discrepancy with competing investigations appropriate to the same unresolved vascular problem.

Keep the necessary new symptoms and study coverage, but avoid an explicit 'not examined' statement functioning as the entire answer. Do not replace valid coverage evidence with vague 'negative scan' wording.

title: Symptom control versus thyroid-hormone production

cues.phrase: Since starting propranolol her pulse and tremor have improved, but free T4 remains above the laboratory interval.
cues.why: Provides the symptom-versus-hormone contrast almost as a teaching sentence; simply increasing the same symptom drug is a weak competing plan.

cues.phrase: has not started another thyroid treatment
cues.why: An explicit missing-treatment cue points to initiating the only new nonradioactive thyroid medicine.

fairness: Methimazole is a defensible treatment to address ongoing Graves hyperthyroidism, subject to clinical review. The task is not a full perioperative optimization plan and does not establish readiness for elective surgery.

Importance: high-yield endocrine/perioperative principle. Realism: endocrine coordination is appropriate. Breastfeeding is a legitimate constraint and must remain; the issue is the weak pair of competitors, not the presence of the constraint. Too easy for residents: two familiar facts do not create two consequential reasoning steps here.
undefined Lactation makes the radioiodine option a clinically excluded competitor; recognizing that requires medical knowledge, so it is a difficulty weakness rather than a purely lexical cue.
suggestions: Compare credible antithyroid or perioperative plans using an actual response trajectory or treatment limitation, with all choices addressing hormone control at the same stage.
Retain lactation status and necessary treatment history, but replace the already-effective symptom-drug escalation and contraindicated treatment as easy foils.

title: IVC filter versus anticoagulation for a provoked DVT

cues.phrase: with no therapeutic regimen entered
cues.why: Names the missing action directly; the key starts 'Therapeutic enoxaparin'.

cues.phrase: Preventive enoxaparin with a retrievable IVC filter
cues.why: Pairs a newly documented clot with the same prevention category already described, making an obviously incomplete treatment foil.

fairness: Therapeutic anticoagulation without routine filter placement is defensible for the supplied postoperative proximal DVT. However, exact enoxaparin selection assumes suitable renal function and no relevant heparin contraindication; those are not provided. The multiple no-bleeding observations are legitimate anticoagulation-safety context, but together they remove the main filter rationale rather than create a close competing decision.

Importance: very high-yield postoperative VTE management. Realism: appropriate hospital escalation; new unilateral symptoms and objective ultrasound are coherent. Too easy once active bleeding and limb threat have both been explicitly neutralized; the dominant rule is anticoagulate an established clot.
suggestions: Use an actual anticoagulation constraint, interruption or apparent treatment-failure question with sufficient dosing/renal/bleeding context to compare plausible plans.
Do not remove safety observations to make filter use ambiguous. If retaining this as a basic VTE safety decision, seek explicit acceptance of that role.

title: Investigating oxygen-carrying capacity

cues.phrase: Copied from the preoperative sample into the postoperative calculation
cues.why: Flags the only stale input explicitly; the sole choice measuring that input is the CBC.

cues.phrase: before attributing his fatigue to persistent pulmonary oxygenation failure
cues.why: The task tells the reader to seek the nonpulmonary alternative, making both gas-related distractors less attractive even without interpreting oxygen content.

cues.phrase: Within the reporting laboratory interval
cues.why: The existing arterial oxygen result partly disposes of the ABG competitor; the normal saturation supplies a second reassurance in the same direction.

fairness: A current hemoglobin measurement is appropriate, but the item can be answered by matching an outdated blood value to its replacement test. It does not require understanding saturation versus oxygen-carrying capacity.

Importance: high-yield perioperative physiology; the current data-audit formulation adds limited value. Realism: why an old calculated oxygen-content record exists should be credible. The current oxygen flow or room-air status is unstated; a normal saturation on supplemental oxygen does not exclude persisting pulmonary impairment. CBC priority does not establish that oxygen can be stopped. Too easy.
suggestions: Use a neutral assessment task, provide the current oxygen condition, and require interpretation of current oxygenation and hemoglobin evidence to choose a consequential action.
Avoid explicitly marking one missing/stale input as the answer. Replace capnography with a credible competing assessment if the actual problem is postoperative exertional fatigue.

title: Tissue sampling after inadequate neck FNA

cues.phrase: Contrast CT shows a percutaneous route to its solid portion
cues.why: Gives feasibility permission matching image-guided core biopsy.

cues.phrase: surgical removal would require dissection beside the carotid sheath
cues.why: Preloads the reason to avoid excision and is repeated in the excision option.

cues.phrase: the least invasive next sampling approach
cues.why: With FNA already repeated and intact architecture requested, the lead-in tells the reader to choose the middle invasiveness option rather than compare diagnostic adequacy.

cues.phrase: the pathologist requests intact tissue relationships
cues.why: Supplies the tissue-requirement interpretation, leaving a familiar FNA-versus-core-versus-excision ladder.

fairness: Image-guided core biopsy is plausible for an accessible deep node when further architecture is needed. Open excision can also be justified for some suspected lymphoid processes; the requested degree of architecture and local pathology expectations would affect adequacy.

Importance: useful tissue-acquisition judgment within general surgery. Realism: deep-node procedural risk is real, but the paired access/risk sentences and least-invasive task are heavily engineered to select core. Too easy as written; do not claim core is universally sufficient for lymphoma classification.
suggestions: Ask a neutral next-biopsy decision with a specific unresolved diagnostic requirement and comparable realistic acquisition plans.

Retain true anatomical risk and access observations, but remove rationale-like feasibility permission and the leading 'least invasive' instruction unless invasiveness itself is the explicitly accepted basic objective.

title: Perioperative respiratory acid-base trajectory

cues.phrase: the gastric suction record did not increase during the second interval
cues.why: Directly contradicts the option 'Review increased gastric suction and chloride losses'.

cues.phrase: the chemistry bicarbonate remained elevated
cues.why: Pre-summarizes the trend shown in the table, narrowing the interpretation before the learner reads it.

fairness: The paired values plausibly show baseline alkalemia with a subsequent CO2 rise; reviewing ventilation/gas exchange is a defensible focus. The apparently normal later pH is a useful teaching point, but the task forces a reassessment and the alternatives leave only the markedly changed CO2 pathway.

Importance: very high-yield perioperative acid-base interpretation. Realism: constructed paired gases are internally plausible; reviewing them later in clinic is a retrospective teaching device. Too easy for PGY-2/3 residents because the alternative chloride-loss explanation is explicitly contradicted and no credible compensatory/ventilatory-management error is offered.
suggestions: Keep the paired gases but remove the redundant interpretation and direct negative against a distractor. Compare specific plausible anesthesia investigations or responses that require interpreting the mixed process and its trajectory.
Use neutral acquisition/ventilation observations as needed to distinguish CO2 absorption from inadequate ventilation; do not invent unsupported management thresholds.

title: Reassessing a changing hand burn

cues.phrase: He reports less pain
cues.why: Directly weakens analgesia-focused reassessment, one of only two competitors.

cues.phrase: Burn-center depth and transfer reassessment
cues.why: The key uniquely addresses lesion severity and escalation; the alternatives address comfort or exercises rather than a competing interpretation of the changing wound.

fairness: Updated specialist depth review is sensible. The outer healing versus central deterioration distinction is important, but the task already guarantees burn-center review and asks only which generic topic to emphasize. It does not establish whether transfer, urgent in-person review or a local-care change is actually needed. The pale, dry, minimally blanching and less sensitive center is a straightforward depth-recognition cluster for residents; these necessary findings should remain.

Importance: high-yield burn evolution and hand-function safety. Realism: reassessment during clinic follow-up is appropriate. Timing, extent and local capability would matter for an actual transfer decision. Too easy; all three topics can belong in the same burn review.
suggestions: Ask one concrete next care action and give the timing, distribution and facility context needed to rank credible escalation choices.
Preserve central depth warning signs; do not hide them for difficulty. Seek explicit safety-recognition acceptance if the aim is simply noticing deepening despite less pain.

title: Paired treatments for urgent VKA reversal

cues.phrase: recorded as vomited before absorption
cues.why: An author-supplied absorption conclusion tells the learner the vitamin-K component is missing; the record cannot ordinarily prove zero absorption merely from vomiting.

cues.phrase: gastric suction continued
cues.why: Directly favors the only intravenous vitamin-K choice over repeating the same oral route.

cues.phrase: The first repeat INR was within the reporting interval.
cues.why: Weakens additional factor concentrate, so the two distractors are each explicitly dealt with by the stem.

fairness: Intravenous vitamin K with follow-up is defensible after urgent factor replacement when oral delivery is unreliable. The valuable principle is sustained reversal after transient factor replacement, but the current options reduce it to replacing a vomited oral drug by another route.

Importance: high-yield urgent anticoagulant reversal. Realism: retrospective hospital review is coherent; 'before absorption' is overly certain unless there is specific observed evidence. Too easy for PGY-2/3 residents.
suggestions: Report observed emesis and medication administration timing without asserting complete nonabsorption. Keep genuine route limitations.

Test the need for sustained reversal despite an initially corrected INR against credible follow-up strategies; avoid making route choice alone identify the key. Supply any decision-critical subsequent INR or bleeding course from supported, clearly constructed data.

title: Rapid VKA factor replacement

cues.phrase: continued arterial extravasation into the abdomen
cues.why: Establishes ongoing major bleeding; the only immediate option is favored over two options expressly delaying reversal.

cues.phrase: no factor concentrate had been given
cues.why: Names the missing intervention that all options repeat, leaving only 'now' versus waiting.

cues.phrase: Give four-factor PCC now with the paired vitamin-K regimen
cues.why: Only the key includes the already-established paired regimen and immediate action; both distractors postpone the same PCC treatment for unrelated or slower responses.

fairness: Urgent factor replacement is a defensible principle in ongoing major warfarin-associated bleeding. However, 'above the laboratory interval' spans minimally elevated through markedly prolonged INR and is insufficiently precise for an exact reversal decision under many protocols; the actual INR and timing relative to vitamin K require clinician review.

Importance: very high-yield emergency reversal. Realism: simultaneous hemorrhage control matters; PCC cannot substitute for control of arterial bleeding. Too easy because the task and options have already selected the agent, leaving an obvious urgent-versus-delay decision.
suggestions: Provide the actual clinically relevant INR/administration chronology and source-supported protocol context without inventing a threshold.

Compare credible immediate reversal strategies or a real residual reversal decision, keeping hemorrhage control concurrent. Alternatively explicitly accept the item as basic urgent-recognition training.

title: Early nutrition after an extensive burn

cues.phrase: Low-rate enteral nutrition with tolerance checks
cues.why: The key uniquely offers cautious initiation of the physiologic route, whereas the alternatives choose primary PN or an explicit stool prerequisite. The reassuring row and 'with tolerance checks' make it the obvious cautious plan.

cues.phrase: Deferred nutritional delivery until stool passage
cues.why: States an absolute gating rule and offers no interim nutrition, making it a weak distractor for a resident.

fairness: The learner does perform two meaningful steps—recognize improving perfusion rather than rely on the earlier shock state, then choose enteral initiation despite quiet bowel sounds—but both are straightforward with these competitors. Too easy for the intended resident difficulty. The completely favorable second perfusion row is necessary data, not an unfair word-matching clue.

Importance: very high-yield burn/critical-care nutrition. Realism: improving perfusion and absence of concerning abdominal findings support cautious feeding. Extent of burn is not actually given in the presentation, despite the title; clinical review should confirm the nutritional indication and trajectory. No definite key error identified.
suggestions: Keep the actual perfusion trajectory and necessary gastrointestinal findings. Compare plausible enteral initiation/escalation strategies or a genuinely unresolved tolerance decision, rather than primary PN and fasting until stool.
If retained as a basic safety item, label and obtain acceptance of that purpose. Do not manufacture difficulty by removing evidence that shock has resolved.

title: Planned thoracic injury exposure

cues.phrase: posterior mid-thoracic esophageal wall defect
cues.why: The accessibility description directly matches the posterolateral component of the key. The visible image is also titled 'Thoracic localization - posterior orientation'.

cues.phrase: the azygos arch approaches the superior vena cava on the right
cues.why: Directly supplies the right-sided component. Combining 'posterior' and 'right' constructs the key from the four balanced options without substantive operative knowledge.

cues.phrase: A track runs down to a pool in the left pleural space.
cues.why: The description has already distinguished the left dependent pool from the actual defect, neutralizing the intended laterality trap before the resident interprets the image.

fairness: Right posterolateral exposure is defensible for the depicted esophageal and azygos targets in a stabilized patient. The image exists and is readable; the problem is that its description preinterprets the source-versus-pool distinction and the choice set makes simple directional matching sufficient.

Importance: useful trauma/esophageal exposure knowledge, though less commonly applied by a PGY-2/3 than the general perioperative items. Realism: retrospective injury localization is coherent. Contralateral pleural contamination may also need treatment; the question is only about exposure of the two repair targets, not a complete operation. Too easy.
suggestions: Retain accessible anatomical observations but avoid a description that narrates the intended source-versus-dependent-pool inference before it is tested.

Compare credible operative approaches requiring consequences of injury level, vascular involvement and physiological status, rather than merely concatenating side and orientation words. Do not remove safety or localization information needed for one best exposure.
